newsitem.title: USA: US markets up, hopes rise for Republican-led House.
newsitem.headline: US markets up, hopes rise for Republican-led House.

text.p: As Americans headed to the polls to vote, stocks and bonds surged Tuesday morning as Wall Street became less nervous that Democrats would wrestle control of Congress from business-friendly Republicans.
The Presidency, all 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives and one-third of the Senate are up for grabs.

The market has discounted a victory by Democrat incumbent president Bill Clinton and expects Republicans to maintain their slim lead in the Senate. But the battle for control of the U.S. House of Representatives has been hotly-contested.

"The market is quite happy with the GOP keeping control of Congress. A few weeks ago, the Iowa political futures market had forecasted the possibility of the GOP losing the House, but now that probability is down to under 17 percent," said Dean Witter chief investment strategist Peter Canelo.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average surged over 30 points in the first 10 minutes of trading to 6072 and the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond rose 22/32, knocking the yield to 6.61 percent.

The prospect of President Clinton's "coat-tails" sweeping enough fellow Democrats along to win Congressional control had caused stomach-churning on Wall Street recently and hemmed stocks into tight ranges.
House Republicans now hold a 235-198 majority. Democrats need a net gain of 18 seats to take back control of the House.

Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist for Josephthal Lyon & Ross, said the markets feared Democratic control of the House because "right or wrong, Wall Street still perceives Democrats as tax and spend, inflationary and anti-growth."
Market analysts said the especially-powerful combination of Democrat president plus a loyal Congress struck fear in the hearts of investors.

UBS Securities chief economist Paul McCulley said, "Status quo is what the market would like the best. The market likes the prospect of checks and and balances of a Democratic White House and a GOP Congress (which) has delivered fiscal austerity.
"If you basically don't trust politicians, a system where you get them tied up in knots is a good thing," McCulley said.
"So gridlock is a good thing," he said.

Voting booths opened at 0600 EST/1100 GMT in several Eastern states and good weather was expected across most of the country. Experts have been predicting an overall low turnout among the 148 million registered voters.
The first results are expected shortly after polls close at 1800 EST/2300 GMT in Kentucky and Indiana. More details will come an hour later, when seven eastern states report.
Analysts still biting their nails over the outcome of the Congressional races will have to wait several hours longer for results, since there are many key races in the West.
But at least one economist said he won't be waiting up all night despite the hype surrounding the elections.

"To be honest, I'd rather know the outcome of next week's retail sales numbers," said Brian Jones, economist at Salomon Brothers. "In the end, what the bond is going to do depends on what the economy does. It always does and it always will."
